content: How to Use This Course This course is designed to build your mental picture of the Coal Handling Plant's belt conveyor system before you set foot on the physical site. Think of it as downloading the entire system into your mind so that when you arrive, you recognise what you see, understand why it exists, and know where the dangers are. This is a context and awareness course only. It does not teach you how to start, stop, or operate any equipment. You must never attempt any operational action independently without formal training and authorisation from the plant management. After completing this course you will be able to walk around a Coal Handling Plant, identify every major component of the belt conveyor system, understand its role in power generation, and — most importantly — recognise hazardous zones and behaviours that could injure you or others.

What You Will Learn in This Course

content: Purpose of the Belt Conveyor System The belt conveyor is the continuous coal transport pipeline inside the plant — like the bloodstream of the power plant. A thermal power plant burns coal to generate steam, which drives a turbine, which spins a generator to produce electricity. The entire generation cycle depends on one simple but critical requirement: a continuous, uninterrupted supply of coal to the boiler . That is exactly what the belt conveyor system does. It is the internal transportation network that moves coal — hundreds or thousands of tonnes per day — from the point where it is received (the wagon tippler / track hopper) to the coal bunkers located above the boilers. From the bunkers, coal flows down to the pulverisers (mills) that grind it into powder for combustion. Coal Mine / Railway Wagon BELT CONVEYOR SYSTEM (CHP) ← This Course → Coal Bunker & Pulveriser Boiler (Combustion) Turbine & Generator Coal-to-electricity conversion chain — Belt Conveyor is Stage 2 If the belt conveyor stops for any reason — mechanical failure, blockage, power trip, misalignment — coal stops moving. Within minutes, the bunker level drops. Within hours, boiler load has to be reduced. If not restored quickly, the entire generating unit may shut down, causing a loss of hundreds of megawatts from the grid. That is the direct consequence of this system failing. In a typical 500 MW coal-fired unit, the conveyor system must deliver approximately 250–300 tonnes of coal per hour continuously. Any interruption has an immediate, measurable cost — both financial and to the reliability of the power supply.
title: Purpose of the Belt Conveyor System

content: System Flow Integration – End-to-End View Wagon Tippler → Hopper → Feeder → Conveyor → Transfer Points → Coal Bunker → Boiler. The conveyor is not isolated — it is one link in a synchronised chain. Before you can understand the conveyor itself, you need to visualise the complete material flow — the journey coal takes from the moment it arrives at the plant to when it reaches the boiler. Think of it like a factory assembly line: every station depends on the one before it, and supplies the one after it. May include a crusher to reduce lump size. | Overload or underload on conveyor; blockages if lumps are too large. ; Belt Conveyor BC-1 | Carries coal horizontally or at an incline to the transfer tower or directly to the bunker. | Entire downstream coal supply stops. ; Transfer Tower | Junction point where coal moves from one conveyor to another (BC-1 to BC-2). An imbalance at any point — too much coal, too little coal, wrong size coal — travels downstream and amplifies. A senior engineer thinks of the entire chain simultaneously, not just the conveyor belt in front of them.

content: Conveyor Components & Layout A moving belt supported and driven across a structured path — like a moving staircase carrying coal instead of people. Before you can work safely near a belt conveyor, you must be able to name every component, point to it, and describe its function . On a real plant, supervisors will test this knowledge before allowing you near the equipment. Below is a systematic walkthrough of every major component. content: 🔴 Belt The belt is the actual carrying medium — the surface on which coal rests and moves. It is made of multiple layers: rubber covers on top and bottom, with reinforcing fabric plies (nylon, polyester, or steel cords) in between. The belt forms a continuous loop — the top strand carries coal forward; the bottom (return) strand travels empty back to the start. A typical CHP belt is 800–1400 mm wide and can be hundreds of metres long. The belt edge is sharp when damaged. The belt surface can drag anything that contacts it. Never stand on or reach over a moving belt.
title: 🔴 Belt

breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

content: 🔵 Drive Unit (Motor + Gearbox + Drive Pulley) This is the power source of the conveyor. An electric motor (typically 110–500 kW in a CHP) drives a gearbox that reduces speed and increases torque. The gearbox output shaft is connected to the drive pulley (also called the head pulley). The belt wraps around this pulley, and friction between the pulley surface and the belt drives the entire system. The drive pulley is always at the discharge (head) end. Pinch point between belt and drive pulley. Extremely high force — instantly fatal if contacted. Must always have a fixed guard.
title: 🔵 Drive Unit (Motor + Gearbox + Drive Pulley)

breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

content: 🟡 Idlers Idlers are the support rollers that keep the belt in shape and prevent it from sagging under the weight of coal. They are spaced every 1–1.5 metres along the top (carry) strand. Carry idlers are usually mounted in a 3-roll troughing configuration to form a trough shape. Return idlers support the empty belt on the return path and are usually flat or slightly tilted. Idlers rotate freely, reducing friction on the belt. Failed (seized) idlers can cause friction, heat, and fire. They also cause belt misalignment. A spinning idler can trap cloth or fingers.
title: 🟡 Idlers

breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

content: ⚪ Tail Pulley Located at the loading (start) end of the conveyor. The tail pulley is a plain pulley — it does not drive the belt. Its role is simply to act as the return point where the belt loops back. The feed point (where coal drops from the hopper/feeder) is usually just after the tail pulley. The tail pulley is also where belt tension is lowest, making slippage in this region less dangerous — but still a pinch hazard.
title: ⚪ Tail Pulley

breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

content: 🟣 Take-up System The belt, like any loop under load, must be kept at the correct tension — not too tight, not too loose. If tension is too low, the belt slips on the drive pulley. If too high, bearings and structure are overloaded. The take-up system maintains this tension automatically. In a gravity take-up , a weighted carriage pulls the tail pulley backward using gravity. In a screw take-up , the tail pulley position is adjusted manually. In heavy-duty conveyors, an automatic hydraulic or winch-type take-up is used.
title: 🟣 Take-up System

breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

content: 🟤 Feed Point (Loading Zone) This is where coal is loaded from the hopper or feeder onto the belt. The feed point includes impact idlers (heavier-duty rollers to absorb the impact of falling coal) and skirt boards (rubber or steel side walls that contain the coal on the belt as it is loaded and prevent spillage at the edges). The alignment and height of the drop point critically affects belt loading quality. Spillage is highest at feed points. Wet or fine coal can also block the skirt boards, causing pressure on the belt edge.
title: 🟤 Feed Point (Loading Zone)

breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

content: 🟠 Scrapers & Belt Cleaners After coal is discharged at the head pulley, a thin layer of fine coal adheres to the belt surface and carries back on the return strand. This is called carryback . Scrapers are blades pressed against the belt surface (at the head pulley and along the return path) to remove this carryback. Without effective scrapers, carryback falls off along the return path, causing spillage, dust, and idler fouling everywhere under the belt.
title: 🟠 Scrapers & Belt Cleaners

breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

content: 🔷 Structure, Walkways & Guards The conveyor is mounted on a steel frame (truss or box structure) that keeps everything aligned and at the correct height. Walkways run alongside for inspection. Nip guards are fitted at all pulley-belt contact points. Emergency pull cords (emergency stop cables) run the full length of the conveyor — pulling the cord anywhere on the conveyor stops it immediately. These are life-saving devices and must never be bypassed. If you see a guard removed or a pull cord damaged, report it immediately. These are mandatory safety devices.
title: 🔷 Structure, Walkways & Guards

content: Functional Mechanism of Conveying Friction-driven continuous loop — the motor grips the belt through the drive pulley; the belt carries coal through friction between coal and rubber surface; idlers support the weight. Understanding how the conveyor actually works — not just what its parts are — is essential to understanding why things go wrong. The entire mechanism depends on three interacting forces: tension, friction, and gravity . MOTOR AC Electric 110–500 kW Coupling GEARBOX Reduces speed Increases torque shaft DRIVE PULLEY → Belt carries coal this way → COAL Idlers (support) TAIL PULLEY ← Return strand (empty belt) ← KEY: Friction at Drive Pulley Pulley surface grips belt → belt moves Tight side tension (High — pulling belt) Slack side tension (Low — returning belt) Take-up (Tension)
title: Functional Mechanism of Conveying

child_titles: The Three Pillars of Conveyor Motion

content: The Three Pillars of Conveyor Motion Force / Principle | What It Does | If Disturbed ; Friction (Drive) | The motor turns the drive pulley; the rubber surface of the pulley grips the belt through friction and pulls it forward. Higher friction coating (lagging) on the pulley increases grip. | If coal, water, or grease gets on the pulley surface, friction is lost → belt slips → coal stops moving → pulley overheats. ; Belt Tension | The take-up system maintains a minimum tension in the belt so the belt wraps tightly around the drive pulley. This ensures the friction force can be transmitted effectively. | Too low tension → belt slips on pulley. Too high → bearing overload, structure damage, belt stretch. ; Idler Support | Idlers distribute the weight of the coal-loaded belt across the structure, reducing the effective force the motor must overcome. They also maintain belt shape (troughing). | Failed idler → belt sags → uneven load → increased friction → motor overload → fire risk. The belt tension is not equal everywhere. On the tight side (belt leaving the drive pulley on the carry strand), tension is high — the belt is being pulled. On the slack side (belt returning to the drive pulley), tension is lower. The difference between these two tensions is what propels the belt and coal forward. This concept explains why adequate take-up tension is so critical — insufficient slack-side tension means the drive pulley cannot transmit enough force.
title: The Three Pillars of Conveyor Motion

content: Why the Belt Drifts (Misalignment) The belt naturally tends to drift (wander sideways) if there is any asymmetry — uneven loading, idlers not perfectly perpendicular to belt travel, wind, or a bent frame. Even a slight drift accumulates over the length of the belt. If not corrected, the belt edge contacts the conveyor structure, causing edge damage, spillage, and ultimately belt failure. Self-aligning idlers and training idlers are used to correct drift automatically. A drifted belt that contacts the steel structure can generate enough heat through friction to ignite coal dust — causing a conveyor fire. Belt fires in CHP are a major risk and have caused plant outages lasting weeks.
title: Why the Belt Drifts (Misalignment)

content: Conveyor Capacity & Throughput Think of capacity as a "pipe size" — the pipe can carry only so much per second. Push more in than it can carry, and it overflows. Push less, and the plant is underfed. Every belt conveyor is designed to carry a specific maximum tonnage per hour (TPH) . This is called the rated capacity. The conveyor design — belt width, speed, inclination, and idler spacing — is optimised for this rated capacity. Operating at or above this limit causes problems; operating well below causes inefficiency.
title: Conveyor Capacity & Throughput

content: Factors That Determine Capacity Factor | How It Affects Capacity | Typical Values (CHP) ; Belt Width | Wider belt = larger cross-sectional area of coal = more tonnes per metre of belt. A wider belt also tolerates larger coal lumps. | 800 mm, 1000 mm, 1200 mm, 1400 mm ; Belt Speed | Higher speed moves the same cross-section faster → more TPH. But higher speed increases dust, wear, and impact at feed points. | 1.2 – 2.5 m/s (typical CHP); up to 4 m/s (high-capacity) ; Trough Angle | Steeper trough (e.g. 35° vs 20°) holds more coal per cross-section. Most CHP conveyors use 35° troughing. | 20°, 25°, 30°, 35°, 45° ; Coal Density & Moisture | Wet coal is heavier per volume → higher tonnage for same volume. However, wet fine coal also sticks to the belt (carryback) and blocks chutes. | Dry coal: ~800 kg/m³; Wet: 900–1000 kg/m³ ; Inclination Angle | Inclined conveyors carry less coal per hour than flat ones at the same belt speed (gravity opposes motion). Steep inclines also risk coal rolling back if belt speed drops. | Max practical: 15°–18° for coal; beyond this, cleated belts needed ; Feed Rate from Feeder | If the upstream feeder delivers more coal than the conveyor is rated for, the belt will be overloaded regardless of its rated capacity. | Controlled via feeder speed (variable frequency drive) When a conveyor is overloaded: (1) coal spills over the belt edges; (2) the motor draws excess current and may trip on overload protection; (3) the belt sags between idlers, increasing friction; (4) the drive may slip; (5) structural stress on the frame increases. Repeated overloading shortens belt life significantly. Underloading (running a conveyor almost empty) wastes electrical energy and accelerates belt wear due to the constant flexing of an unloaded belt over idlers. It also reduces the effective cleaning action of belt cleaners and increases dust generation from the empty belt vibrating on return idlers. A 500 MW thermal unit needs approximately 250–300 TPH of coal at full load. If the belt conveyor can carry 400 TPH rated capacity, there is a buffer. If an upstream crusher or feeder fails and reduces supply to 150 TPH, the bunker level gradually falls and load must be reduced. An intern does not control these rates — but understanding this relationship lets you understand the urgency when a supervisor responds to a falling bunker level.
title: Factors That Determine Capacity

content: Transfer Points & Flow Behaviour A transfer point is like a controlled handover baton pass — coal must land precisely on the next belt. Any miss, blockage, or misalignment at this point disrupts the entire downstream flow. Wherever coal moves from one conveyor to the next — or from a hopper to a conveyor — there is a transfer point . These are not minor connections; they are among the most critical and most hazardous locations in the entire Coal Handling Plant. Understanding what happens at a transfer point is essential before entering the CHP. BC-1 (Upper Conveyor) Coal on BC-1 Head Pulley TRANSFER CHUTE (guides coal) ↓ Coal falls here BC-2 (Lower Conveyor) Impact Zone Coal on BC-2 ⚠ DUST ⚠ Spillage ⚠ Spillage ⚠ BLOCKAGE RISK Wet/sticky coal can block chute Coal must land centrally on BC-2 belt. Any deviation → spillage or belt drift.
title: Transfer Points & Flow Behaviour

content: What Can Go Wrong at a Transfer Point Problem | Cause | Consequence ; Chute Blockage | Wet, fine, or sticky coal accumulates inside the chute and sticks to walls, eventually bridging across. | Coal backs up onto BC-1, causing it to overload. If blockage is not cleared quickly, the conveyor trips. ; Spillage | Coal falls outside the belt edges due to misaligned chute, worn skirt boards, or over-speed discharge. | Accumulation of coal on walkways and structure — slipping hazard, fire risk from dust, structural overloading. ; Dust Generation | Free-fall of coal creates turbulent air that carries fine coal particles. Longer drop height = more dust. | Respiratory hazard, reduced visibility, fire and explosion risk from coal dust cloud. ; Belt Damage at Impact | Large coal lumps falling from height impact the belt at the transfer point, especially if impact idlers are worn. | Belt cover damage, gouging, or even belt puncture — leading to belt failure. ; Off-centre Loading | Coal does not land centrally on BC-2 due to incorrect chute alignment or spillage plate wear. | Belt drifts to one side → edge damage → spillage → potential belt damage against structure. Transfer towers are enclosed structures at junctions between conveyors. They are high-dust, confined-space environments with active machinery on multiple levels. Entry requires a Confined Space Entry Permit, dust mask, and must always be done with a buddy. Never enter during conveyor operation without a specific maintenance permit.

content: Safety & Hazard Awareness Moving machinery + bulk material + confined spaces = continuous risk. Most conveyor accidents happen not because of complexity but because someone was not aware of where the danger was. You do not need to be doing anything wrong to be injured near a conveyor. You simply need to be in the wrong place, distracted, or unaware of what is moving around you. The conveyor does not slow down for you. It does not have a sensor that detects a human body near it. It will continue running at full speed regardless. Your awareness is your protection. content: Hazard-by-Hazard Analysis Pulleys rotate continuously at high speed. The nip point — where the belt meets the pulley — has an extremely small gap that closes in milliseconds. A finger, loose clothing, or hair entering this gap will be drawn in with full motor force before any human reaction is possible. Guards (physical covers) must always be in place over all pulleys. If a guard is missing — report it immediately and do not approach the pulley. The belt surface itself is a hazard. Loose clothing, gloves, tools, or anything trailing near the belt can be instantly grabbed and pulled in. Belt speed (1.5–2.5 m/s) is faster than human reflex. This type of accident typically results in degloving injuries, crush injuries, or fatalities. Rule: always wear close-fitting PPE near conveyors. Never lean over a running belt. At transfer points, coal falls from one conveyor to the next. Large coal lumps weighing several kilograms can bounce or be thrown sideways if a blockage or imbalance occurs. Standing below or beside an active chute is extremely dangerous. Transfer towers also have open floors and structural walkways at multiple levels — falling coal from one level can injure personnel on a lower level. Fine coal dust generated at transfer points, feed points, and from carryback is a dual hazard. Respiratory: Coal dust causes coal worker's pneumoconiosis (CWP/"black lung") with long-term exposure. Always wear a P2/P3 dust mask in dusty areas. Fire: Coal dust suspended in air at concentrations above the Lower Explosive Limit (LEL) can ignite from a spark or hot surface. Accumulated coal dust on hot surfaces (like a seized idler or a slipping belt) can also self-ignite. Coal spillage on walkways creates an extremely slippery surface, especially when wet. Carryback coal falls from the return strand onto the floor below the conveyor. Structural platforms, stairs, and walkways in CHP are often narrow and positioned close to moving equipment. Falls from elevated walkways (transfer towers can be 10–20 m high) are fatal. Always hold handrails, wear non-slip safety boots, and never rush on CHP walkways. Conveyor drive panels operate at medium voltage (3.3 kV or 6.6 kV in large plants, 415 V in smaller). Control panels, junction boxes, and local isolators are located along conveyor routes. Never open an electrical panel without a qualified electrician present and without following Lockout-Tagout (LOTO) procedures. Water from coal spillage near electrical panels is extremely dangerous.
title: Hazard-by-Hazard Analysis

You will never be penalised for pulling the emergency cord in a genuine emergency.

content: Types of Wagon Tippler – Upstream Context The wagon tippler is the starting gun — the moment coal enters the plant. Different tippler types deliver coal at different rates, lump sizes, and patterns, each with a different impact on the first belt conveyor. Coal arrives at a thermal power plant in railway wagons — each carrying 60–80 tonnes of coal. The wagon tippler is the mechanism that unloads these wagons. The type of tippler directly affects: How quickly coal is unloaded (feed rate) The lump size of coal entering the hopper The loading pattern on the first belt conveyor Dust generation at the unloading point Three Main Types of Wagon Unloading Systems ① Rotary Tippler WAGON HOPPER 150–160° rotation Rotary Tippler Wagon rotated 150–160° on a circular cradle. Wagon stays on rail. Fastest method. Capacity: 1 wagon/12–20 min ⚠ High dust at discharge ② Side Discharge Tippler WAGON HOPPER 45–60° side tilt Side Discharge Tippler Wagon tilts to one side on a pivoted platform. Slower but gentler on the wagon body. Used for bottom-discharge wagons ⚠ Uneven coal distribution ③ Track Hopper System WAGON (No rotation) ↓ Bottom doors ↓ open gravity Grated Track PIT HOPPER Track Hopper System Wagon moves over a grated pit. Bottom-discharge wagons drop coal directly. No tippler. Fastest — continuous unloading ✓ Lowest dust among three types
title: Types of Wagon Tippler – Upstream Context

content: Comparison Table Feature | Rotary Tippler | Side Discharge Tippler | Track Hopper ; Unloading Method | Rotates wagon 150–160° | Tilts wagon sideways 45–60° | Bottom-discharge through grates ; Wagon Type Required | Any (standard BOX-N wagons) | Side-door wagons | Bottom-discharge BOBR/BOXN-HL wagons ; Unloading Speed | Moderate (12–20 min/wagon) | Slow (20–30 min/wagon) | Fast — continuous ; Coal Lump Size | Can break lumps on impact | Less impact — larger lumps retained | Large lumps pass through grate ; Dust Generation | High (coal falls from height) | Moderate | Low (enclosed pit) ; Feed Consistency | Batch — surge then pause | Batch — gradual | Near-continuous with flow control ; Impact on Conveyor | Surge loading — needs robust feed control | More manageable surges | Steady, easiest on conveyor ; Typical Use in India | Most common (NTPC, APGENCO, etc.) | Older plants | Modern large plants When a rotary tippler unloads a wagon, coal arrives at the hopper in a surge — a large volume in a short time — followed by a pause as the next wagon is positioned. This surge must be absorbed by the hopper before it reaches the feeder and then the belt. If the hopper is small or the feeder is not controlled properly, the surge can overload the belt. Conversely, during the changeover between wagons, the belt may run empty. This cyclic loading is normal for rotary tippler plants, and belt systems are designed to handle it — but a new intern should understand why the loading on the belt appears uneven.

content: Critical Process Control Points Control points are the locations in the system where the quality, continuity, and safety of coal flow are most sensitive. These are the points a plant engineer monitors most carefully. As an intern, you will hear these terms constantly — understanding what they mean is essential.
title: Critical Process Control Points

content: Coal Loading onto Belt (Feed Point) Where: Just after the tail pulley, where coal from the hopper/feeder drops onto the moving belt. What is critical here: The coal must be deposited centrally on the belt, at a controlled rate (not exceeding rated TPH), and with minimum free-fall height to reduce impact and dust. Skirt boards must form a tight seal at the edges to contain coal. Any gap in the skirt board → immediate spillage. Overloading at CP-1 causes belt sag, edge spillage, and motor overload. Blocked skirt boards cause belt edge damage. Impact from large coal lumps at feed point damages belt cover.
title: Coal Loading onto Belt (Feed Point)

breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

content: Transfer Between Conveyors (Transfer Point) Where: Transfer tower — where coal discharges from BC-1 and loads onto BC-2 through a chute. What is critical here: The trajectory of coal through the chute must be matched to the receiving belt speed and direction. The coal must land centrally on BC-2. The chute must be free of blockage. Chute liners (wear-resistant steel plates) must be intact. Deflector plates must direct coal accurately. This is the highest-risk location in the entire CHP. Blockages here can back-fill the chute, causing BC-1 overload. Spillage from here falls from height. Dust is at maximum. Confined space entry here requires a formal permit.
title: Transfer Between Conveyors (Transfer Point)

content: Belt Movement at Drive Pulley Where: Head end of conveyor — drive pulley, motor, gearbox assembly. What is critical here: The drive pulley must maintain sufficient friction with the belt to transmit motor torque without slipping. The belt must wrap around the pulley at the correct arc (wrap angle). The head scraper must effectively remove coal from the belt surface as it discharges. The belt must discharge coal cleanly into the chute below. Extreme mechanical hazard zone. The nip point here has the highest torque in the system. Guard must always be in place. Belt slip here causes overheating and fire. Scraper failure leads to carryback and belt underside fouling.
title: Belt Movement at Drive Pulley

breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

content: Belt Alignment Along Structure Where: Monitored continuously along the full length of the conveyor using belt sway switches. What is critical here: The belt must remain centred on the idlers throughout its full length. Belt sway switches are installed at regular intervals — if the belt drifts beyond a set limit, the sway switch first gives an alarm; if drift continues, it trips the conveyor. Self-aligning (training) idlers automatically correct minor drift. Regular inspection of idler alignment and condition is essential to maintaining belt tracking. Belt drift → edge contact with structure → friction heat → fire risk. Spillage along the full belt length. Edge damage requires expensive belt replacement.
title: Belt Alignment Along Structure

breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

content: Discharge at Coal Bunker Where: Head end of the final conveyor — above the coal bunker. What is critical here: Coal must discharge into the correct bunker bay. In large plants, a tripper car (a movable discharge device on the belt) distributes coal across multiple bunker bays to maintain even filling. Bunker level indicators monitor how full each bay is. If a bunker overflows, coal falls into the boiler bay — a serious fire and housekeeping hazard. If a bunker starves, the boiler load must be reduced immediately. Bunker overflow → coal on boiler bay floor → fire risk near hot surfaces. Bunker starvation → forced load reduction → revenue loss. Dust in bunker bay is particularly hazardous — bunker bays are semi-enclosed high-dust zones.

content: 👷 Human Safety Entanglement in moving belt → degloving, amputation, fatality Entanglement in drive pulley nip → instant, irreversible crush injury Falling coal at transfer point → blunt trauma, fracture Belt fire → smoke inhalation, burn injuries Coal dust explosion → blast and burn injuries across large area Slipping on coal spillage → fall from height in transfer towers (potentially fatal) Electrical contact near damaged panels → electrocution Every failure in this list was, at some point, preventable . The difference between a major accident and a near-miss is often one person who was paying attention and reported what they saw. content: Uneven Loading → Belt Drift → Structural Damage Cause: Coal from the feeder drops consistently to one side of the belt (e.g., feeder gate partially blocked, chute misaligned). The belt carries more load on one side than the other. What Happens: The belt gradually drifts toward the heavier side. It contacts the steel frame of the conveyor structure. Friction between the belt edge and the frame generates heat. Over hours, the belt edge begins to abrade. Coal spillage begins at the affected side. If not corrected, the belt tears longitudinally — a full-length split requiring complete belt replacement. Early Signs: Belt sway alarm activates. Visible drift at one or more idler sets. Spillage on one side only. Squealing noise from belt-structure contact. Consequence: Forced conveyor shutdown. Belt replacement cost (₹10–40 lakhs). 2–5 days of downtime for re-belting.
title: Uneven Loading → Belt Drift → Structural Damage

content: Overloading → Belt Stress → Spillage → Motor Trip Cause: The feeder speed is set too high, or a sudden surge from the wagon tippler overwhelms the hopper. Coal falls on the belt at a rate exceeding rated capacity. What Happens: Coal piles up on the belt, exceeding the trough capacity. Spillage occurs from both edges. The belt sags more between idlers, increasing rolling resistance. Motor current rises. Motor protection relay detects overload and trips the motor. The belt stops. Coal continues to fall from the hopper onto the stationary belt, burying it under a pile of coal. Early Signs: High motor current alarm. Increased spillage at feed point. Belt visibly overloaded (coal reaching edge of trough). Vibration increase. Consequence: Conveyor buried under coal. Manual digging-out required (hours of labour). Belt may be damaged under the weight. Entire coal flow stopped.
title: Overloading → Belt Stress → Spillage → Motor Trip

content: Poor Transfer Point Flow → Chute Blockage → System Shutdown Cause: Wet, fine coal (after rain or due to high moisture content) builds up on the inner walls of the transfer chute. Over time, coal bridges across the chute opening. What Happens: Coal flow through the chute reduces, then stops. BC-1 continues running — coal piles up at the head pulley discharge point and overflows the chute. BC-2 runs empty, drawing coal from the bunker without being replenished. Bunker level falls. Eventually, BC-1 is tripped on overload as coal piles up. The plant is called to reduce load. Early Signs: BC-2 belt running empty (visible drop in load current). Spillage at base of transfer chute. Unusual noise from chute (hollow sound instead of coal flow sound). Consequence: Manual chute cleaning required. Confined space permit needed. Risk of coal avalanche when blockage suddenly clears.
title: Poor Transfer Point Flow → Chute Blockage → System Shutdown

content: Belt Slipping on Drive Pulley → Loss of Conveying → Overheating Cause: Water or coal slurry contaminates the surface of the drive pulley, reducing friction. Or the take-up tension is insufficient. The belt cannot maintain grip on the rotating pulley. What Happens: The drive pulley continues to rotate, but the belt slips — moving slower than the pulley surface. This generates significant heat at the pulley-belt contact zone. The rubber lagging on the pulley begins to burn. Acrid smoke is generated. If the conveyor is not stopped, the lagging is destroyed, and eventually the belt itself can ignite. Meanwhile, coal stops moving because the belt is stationary or barely moving. Early Signs: Burning rubber smell. Smoke from head end. Reduced belt speed indicator. High motor current (motor is working hard but belt is not moving at designed speed). Consequence: Belt fire — major safety incident. Drive pulley lagging replacement. Potential partial belt damage. 1–3 days outage.
title: Belt Slipping on Drive Pulley → Loss of Conveying → Overheating

content: Dust Accumulation Ignition → Conveyor Fire Cause: Coal dust accumulates on conveyor structure, idlers, and the underside of the belt over weeks without adequate housekeeping. A seized idler generates frictional heat. This heat ignites the accumulated coal dust. What Happens: Smouldering begins on the structure or inside the belt tunnel. Because coal dust is distributed over a large area, the fire can spread rapidly along the full length of the conveyor. In an enclosed conveyor (gallery), fire and smoke can develop quickly. A conveyor fire can destroy the entire belt (hundreds of metres long), the structure, and adjacent equipment. Early Signs: Burning smell. Smoke in the conveyor gallery. Seized idler (idler not rotating despite belt moving — creates a flat worn spot on the idler and local heating). Unusual hotspot detected by thermal camera. Consequence: Major fire incident. Full belt replacement. Structural repairs. Plant outage of weeks. Regulatory investigation. Possible fatalities if personnel are in the gallery.
title: Dust Accumulation Ignition → Conveyor Fire

content: Exposure to Moving Parts → Entanglement Injury Cause: A person reaches over or near a running conveyor without adequate clearance. Loose clothing, gloves, or hair contacts the moving belt or a rotating idler/pulley. What Happens: The belt instantly grips the material and draws the person's limb or clothing into the nip point. At 1.5 m/s belt speed and with a motor delivering hundreds of kilowatts, the force is thousands of times greater than human strength. No one can pull free. The injury is instantaneous and typically irreversible — degloving, crush, amputation, or fatal entrapment. Prevention: Guard all nip points (mandatory, not optional). Never approach a running conveyor without proper authorisation. Emergency pull cord must be functional and tested. Buddy system — never work alone near running equipment. Consequence: Serious injury or fatality. Plant shutdown for investigation. Management liability. Irreparable human loss. There is zero tolerance in a professional plant for bypassing guards, reaching over running conveyors, or working near running equipment without proper PPE and procedures. This is not bureaucracy — it is the direct lesson from real fatalities.

content: Instrumentation & Safety Devices on the Conveyor Think of instrumentation as the conveyor's nervous system — sensors spread across the full length that continuously sense abnormal conditions and either warn operators or automatically stop the machine before a small problem becomes a catastrophe. A belt conveyor in a modern Coal Handling Plant is fitted with numerous sensors, switches, and protective devices along its entire length. These are not optional extras — they are mandatory safety and operational requirements under Indian Electricity Rules, factory safety regulations, and plant operating procedures. As an intern, you will see these devices everywhere on the conveyor. Knowing what each one does is essential. content: Safety Device Reference Guide Device | Location on Conveyor | Function | Response When Activated ; Emergency Pull Cord (EPC) | Both sides, full length of conveyor, approximately every 30–50 m | Allows any person anywhere along the conveyor to immediately stop it in an emergency by pulling the rope/wire | Immediate emergency stop of conveyor drive motor. Conveyor cannot restart until EPC is reset and root cause investigated. ; Belt Sway Switch (BSW) | Both sides, spaced every 50–75 m along carry and return strand | Detects lateral drift of the belt beyond a set limit. Has two positions: first position = alarm; second position = trip. | First activation: Alarm in control room. Second (greater drift): Conveyor trip. Prevents belt edge from contacting steel structure. ; Zero Speed Switch (ZSS) | Tail pulley shaft or on a return idler | Monitors belt speed. Detects if the belt has stopped (zero speed) while the motor is still running — indicating belt slip. | Conveyor trip + alarm. Prevents drive pulley from running against a stationary belt (which causes fire from friction). ; Belt Weigher (BW) | Fixed location on the conveyor, typically mid-span | Measures the weight of coal on the belt per unit length using load cells. Calculates instantaneous TPH and cumulative tonnes. | Data sent to control room / DCS. No trip — provides operational data. High load may trigger an alarm. ; Chute Blocked Detector (CBD) | Inside transfer chutes at transfer points | Detects when coal has accumulated and blocked the chute (using vibration probe, ultrasonic, or paddle switch). | Alarm in control room. May automatically stop upstream feeder to prevent further coal accumulation. ; Thermal / Fire Detector | Inside conveyor galleries (tunnels) and transfer towers | Detects elevated temperature indicating a developing fire. Linear heat detection cable runs along the belt gallery roof. | Fire alarm. Conveyor trip. Activation of fire suppression system (CO₂ or water mist). Control room alert. ; Underspeed Switch | Drive shaft area | Detects if belt is running slower than designed speed (but not zero). Indicates overloading or drive slip developing. | Alarm → trip if underspeed persists. Allows early intervention before full slippage occurs. ; Motor Overload Relay (OLR) | Motor control centre (MCC) / switchgear panel | Monitors motor current. If the motor draws current above the rated limit for a set time (indicating overload), it trips. | Motor trip + alarm. Conveyor stops. Investigation required to identify overload cause before restart. When you walk a conveyor on site, you will see red ropes, yellow boxes, and small switches mounted on the frame at regular intervals — these are all part of this safety system. You will hear terms like "BSW trip," "ZSS alarm," or "EPC activation" on the radio constantly. Now you know exactly what each term means, what triggered it, and what the plant team needs to do in response. On some plants, under production pressure, well-meaning but incorrect actions include bypassing a belt sway switch that keeps tripping, disabling a chute blocked detector that gives "false" alarms, or tying off an EPC that was accidentally pulled. This is an extremely dangerous practice. Every safety device bypass removes one layer of protection from the system. Multiple bypasses create a condition where a fatal accident can occur without any warning. As an intern, if you are ever asked to bypass a safety device, immediately consult your supervisor. Document it. Never accept it as routine.

content: Your First Site Visit – What to Observe & What to Look For Your first site visit is not a tour — it is a structured observation exercise. For every component you studied in this course, there is a physical object in front of you. Treat it like matching a textbook diagram to a real machine, component by component. Now that you understand the system theoretically, you need to translate that knowledge to what you will actually see, hear, and smell when you walk into the Coal Handling Plant for the first time. This guide prepares you for that transition, so you do not feel overwhelmed or miss important details. Site Visit Observation Sequence – Walk the Conveyor Like an Engineer STEP 1 Start at the Feed Point (Tail End) Observe loading STEP 2 Walk Along One Side of Belt Check belt & idlers STEP 3 Observe Drive / Head End Check discharge STEP 4 Look at Safety Devices EPC, sway switches STEP 5 Visit Transfer Tower (outside) Observe from safe zone STEP 6 – REFLECT & REPORT Note all abnormalities observed. Discuss with supervisor. NEVER act on abnormalities independently. ⛔ NEVER do this on your first visit: Do not touch, adjust, or interfere with any equipment — observe only.

Skirt boards are close to the belt surface with no visible gap. No coal spillage outside the belt edges. Dust suppression sprays (if fitted) are operating. | Coal spilling over belt edges. Gap between skirt board and belt. Coal piling up at sides. Dust cloud larger than usual. Unusual impact noise from large lumps. ; Belt Surface (While Walking Alongside) | Belt is centred on idlers. Surface is intact — no cuts, gouges, or longitudinal slits. Coal is uniformly distributed across the belt width. Belt moves smoothly without lateral wandering. | Belt visibly off-centre (drift). Belt edge near or touching structure. Cuts or rips on belt surface. Uneven coal load (all on one side). Belt flapping or vibrating excessively. ; Idlers (Along the Full Length) | All idlers are spinning freely as the belt passes over them. No noise from any individual idler. No flat spot on any roller (from seizure). All idlers are in their correct mounting position. | Any idler NOT spinning (seized — belt slides over it creating heat). Grinding or squealing noise from an idler bearing. Idler shell worn flat on one spot. Idler hanging loose or displaced from its bracket. ; Structure & Walkway (Below the Belt) | Walkway is clean — minimal coal spillage on the floor. Structure is intact. No coal accumulated on structural members. Return strand is clean (minimal carryback coal on the underside). | Coal accumulated on structural members (fire risk). Excessive carryback falling onto the floor below. Wet coal mix on walkway (slip hazard). Smell of burning rubber or coal smoke. ; Drive / Head End | Coal discharges cleanly over the head pulley into the chute. Belt scraper is in contact with the belt and removing carryback. Head pulley guard is in place. No burning smell. Motor noise is normal (steady hum). | Coal not discharging cleanly (flying off sideways). Burning rubber smell (belt slipping on pulley). Unusual motor noise (overload — grinding or laboured hum). Scraper not in contact with belt. Any guard missing. ; Safety Devices | All EPC ropes are present, unbroken, and at the correct tension (not sagging to ground, not over-tight). Belt sway switches are mounted and free. No safety device is taped up, bypassed, or disabled. | EPC rope broken, missing, or sagging. Sway switch blocked with coal or debris. Any safety device with a bypass tag or wire tied in bypassed position. Missing nip point guards at pulleys. ; Transfer Tower (from outside / entrance) | Coal flow sound is continuous and steady from inside (not intermittent). No coal spillage on the outside of the tower base. Dust seal curtains at openings are intact. | Silence from chute (blockage). Coal spilling from tower base. Dust escaping from every gap (excess spillage inside). Unusual vibration of the tower structure. As an intern, you will not be allowed to operate equipment. But you can walk the conveyors during your inspection rounds with a supervisor, and you can see things that busy operators may have overlooked . A fresh pair of eyes — trained by this course to know what is normal and what is not — can catch an early warning sign that prevents a major failure. Always report what you observe to your supervisor, and never assume "someone else must have seen it already."

content: Do's and Don'ts for the Intern in the Coal Handling Plant This section translates your theoretical learning into specific behaviours. These are not rules imposed on you — they are the behaviours that keep you alive and healthy during your internship and throughout your career in the power industry.
title: Do's and Don'ts for the Intern in the Coal Handling Plant

Do's and Don'ts for the Intern in the Coal Handling Plant

content: ✅ DO – Always ✔ Always wear your complete PPE before entering the CHP area — helmet, boots, high-vis vest, and dust mask at minimum. ✔ Always stay on designated walkways. Never take shortcuts across structural members or below return strands. ✔ Always walk in pairs (buddy system) inside CHP, especially in galleries and near transfer towers. ✔ Always report abnormalities (seized idler, missing guard, damaged EPC) to your supervisor immediately — verbally and in writing. ✔ Always ask for a proper explanation before approaching any equipment you have not previously been briefed on. ✔ Always maintain a minimum clearance of 1 metre from the belt and moving machinery unless you are following a supervised inspection protocol. ✔ Always wear close-fitting clothing. Tuck in shirts. No loose ties, scarves, or dangling lanyards. ✔ Always know the location of the nearest Emergency Pull Cord and fire extinguisher on any conveyor you are walking. ✔ Always pull the EPC without hesitation if you see an entanglement, smoke, or fire — never wait for confirmation.
title: ✅ DO – Always
parent_title: Do's and Don'ts for the Intern in the Coal Handling Plant

Do's and Don'ts for the Intern in the Coal Handling Plant

content: ⛔ DON'T – Never ✘ Never touch a moving belt — not to feel the speed, test the surface, or remove a piece of coal from it. ✘ Never lean over a running conveyor for any reason — not to look at the other side, not to pick up a fallen object. ✘ Never attempt to clear a blocked chute or dislodged coal from a running conveyor using your hands, feet, or tools. ✘ Never remove guards from pulleys or other rotating parts — even "just to check" something. ✘ Never silence or bypass a safety alarm without a supervisor's explicit authorisation and a proper investigation. ✘ Never enter a transfer tower, conveyor gallery, or any confined space without a valid Confined Space Entry Permit. ✘ Never operate any switch, valve, or control on the conveyor unless specifically instructed and supervised by an authorised engineer. ✘ Never work alone in the CHP — especially in conveyor galleries, transfer towers, and tunnels below trestle conveyors. ✘ Never assume a stopped conveyor is safe without confirming it is Locked Out / Tagged Out (LOTO) by a qualified person. One of the most common causes of serious injury in industrial plants is working on equipment that appears to be stopped but is not properly isolated. A conveyor belt that stopped due to an alarm can be restarted from the control room while someone is working on it. The Lockout-Tagout (LOTO) procedure requires the drive to be electrically isolated at the switchgear, locked with a physical padlock, and tagged with the worker's identity before any maintenance work begins. As an intern, you must never approach any equipment for maintenance purposes. If asked to, immediately request that proper LOTO isolation is carried out and confirmed before you go near the equipment.

content: Glossary of CHP & Belt Conveyor Terms On your first day on site you will hear these terms constantly. This glossary ensures you are not lost in the conversation. Term | Meaning ; Belt | The continuous rubber-fabric loop that carries coal from tail to head end. ; Belt Conveyor (BC) | The complete conveyor assembly — numbered in sequence (BC-1, BC-2, etc.) in the plant. ; Carry Strand | The top run of the belt that carries coal toward the discharge point. ; Return Strand | The lower run of the empty belt going back from head to tail. ; Head Pulley | The drive pulley at the discharge end of the conveyor. ; Tail Pulley | The non-driven pulley at the loading end. ; Idler | A free-spinning roller that supports the belt. Troughing idlers (carry) and flat idlers (return). ; Trough Angle | The angle at which wing idler rolls are tilted to form the trough (20°–45°). ; Take-up | The tensioning device — gravity, screw, or hydraulic — that keeps the belt at correct tension. ; Lagging | Rubber coating on the drive pulley surface to increase friction with the belt. ; Skirt Board | Side rubber/steel walls at the feed point that contain coal on the belt edge. ; Scraper / Cleaner | A blade pressed against the belt at the head end to remove carryback coal. ; Carryback | Fine coal that sticks to the belt after discharge and is carried back on the return strand. ; Transfer Point | Location where coal moves from one conveyor to the next via a chute. ; Chute | The steel guide structure that directs coal from one conveyor to the next at transfer points. ; Tripper Car | A movable discharge device on a conveyor above the bunker that distributes coal across bunker bays. Term | Meaning ; Bunker | Large coal storage silo above the boiler, fed by the conveyor. Buffer for continuous boiler feeding. ; Hopper | A funnel-shaped collection vessel below the wagon tippler that collects unloaded coal. ; Feeder | A device (vibrating, apron, or belt type) that controls the rate of coal feeding onto the conveyor. ; TPH | Tonnes Per Hour — the standard unit of conveyor throughput capacity. ; CHP | Coal Handling Plant — the entire system for receiving, processing, and conveying coal in a power plant. ; DCS | Distributed Control System — the central computerised control system monitoring all CHP parameters. ; MCC | Motor Control Centre — the electrical switchgear panel that starts, stops, and protects conveyor motors. ; EPC | Emergency Pull Cord — the safety rope running the full length of the conveyor for emergency stop. ; BSW | Belt Sway Switch — sensor that detects lateral belt drift and triggers alarm/trip. ; ZSS / USS | Zero Speed Switch / Underspeed Switch — detects belt slippage or stall. ; LOTO | Lockout-Tagout — energy isolation procedure before maintenance on conveyor or any equipment. ; Nip Point | The point where the belt meets a pulley — the most dangerous entanglement zone. ; Belt Drift | Lateral wandering of the belt off centre — can cause edge damage and fire. ; Tight Side | The belt strand leaving the drive pulley (carry side) — where belt tension is highest. ; Slack Side | The belt strand returning to the drive pulley — where tension is lower. ; CWP | Coal Workers' Pneumoconiosis — lung disease caused by long-term coal dust inhalation ("black lung").

content: Conveying का Functional Mechanism Belt conveyor एक friction-drive system है — बिल्कुल car के tyre की तरह जो road को grip करके आगे बढ़ता है। Motor घूमता है, drive pulley घूमता है, friction होती है, belt चलती है। यह समझना कि belt physically कैसे चलती है, आपको यह भी समझने में help करेगा कि यह कब और क्यों fail होती है। MOTOR बिजली → घूमना GEAR- BOX DRIVE PULLEY TIGHT SIDE →→→ (High Tension) ←←← SLACK SIDE (कम tension) TAIL PULLEY ① Motor torque pulley को rotate करता है ② Friction → belt move होती है Tight side = pulling force ③ Tail pulley free घूमता है Belt यहाँ से wrap होती है Belt Tension की ज़रूरत क्यों? Tension कम → Drive Pulley की grip कम → Belt Slip → Coal नहीं चलती → Friction Heat → FIRE Tension ज़्यादा → Bearings overload → Structure damage → Belt splice fail

content: Belt Drift — क्यों होती है, क्यों ख़तरनाक है? Belt को हमेशा idlers के centre में रहना चाहिए। लेकिन अगर loading एक side पर ज़्यादा हो, idler alignment off हो, या tension uneven हो — belt धीरे-धीरे एक side की तरफ खिसकने लगती है। इसे belt drift कहते हैं। Belt drift → Belt का edge steel structure से contact → Friction heat generate → Coal dust ignite → FIRE। साथ में spillage पूरी belt length पर, expensive belt replacement, और plant shutdown। Belt sway switches (BSW) automatic alarm और trip देते हैं अगर drift ज़्यादा हो।

content: Conveyor Capacity और Throughput Conveyor capacity एक highway की तरह है — जितना चौड़ा और तेज़, उतना ज़्यादा traffic। लेकिन जैसे highway पर limit होती है, conveyor पर भी rated capacity से ज़्यादा नहीं जा सकते। हर belt conveyor एक specific throughput rate के लिए design किया जाता है जो Tonnes Per Hour (TPH) में measure होती है। यह rating engineers ने carefully calculate की होती है। इससे ज़्यादा coal डालोगे — problems शुरू।
title: Conveyor Capacity और Throughput

child_titles: Capacity किन factors पर निर्भर करती है?

content: Capacity किन factors पर निर्भर करती है? Factor | Effect on Capacity | Practical Range ; Belt Width | चौड़ी belt → ज़्यादा coal per metre carry कर सकती है | 800 mm से 1,400 mm तक (coal CHP में) ; Belt Speed | तेज़ belt → उसी cross-section पर ज़्यादा tonnes per hour | 1.2 से 2.5 m/s typical ; Trough Angle | ज़्यादा angle → ज़्यादा coal hold होती है per metre | 20° से 45° (20° standard, 35°–45° high capacity) ; Inclination | ज़्यादा slope → gravity के against काम → कम effective capacity | Coal के लिए max ~15°–18° (cleated belt के बिना) ; Coal Density | Dense coal → same volume = ज़्यादा weight (tonnes) | 750–950 kg/m³ (moisture पर depend करता है) ; Coal Moisture | Wet coal ज़्यादा heavy, sticky, और blockage-prone होती है | Rainy season में significant impact Overloading: Coal belt के edges से spill होती है → Motor overload → Trip → Conveyor बंद। Coal pile-up को manually साफ़ करना पड़ता है — घंटों का काम। Underloading: Belt half-empty चल रही है → कम TPH → Bunker level गिर रहा है → Boiler को load कम करना पड़ेगा। इसीलिए feeder की speed और hopper level को carefully monitor करते हैं। आप conveyor की rated capacity control नहीं करते — वह तो engineers ने पहले से set कर दी है। लेकिन आपको यह समझना है कि जब belt overloaded दिखे (coal edges तक पहुँच रही हो) या जब belt almost empty चल रही हो — दोनों असामान्य conditions हैं जो supervisor को immediately report करनी चाहिए। इसी awareness के लिए यह course है।
title: Capacity किन factors पर निर्भर करती है?

content: Transfer Points और Coal Flow का व्यवहार Transfer point एक relay race का baton pass है — coal को ठीक अगली belt पर land करना होता है। कोई भी चूक, blockage, या misalignment यहाँ पूरे downstream flow को बाधित कर देती है। जहाँ भी coal एक conveyor से दूसरे पर जाती है — या hopper से conveyor पर — वहाँ एक transfer point होता है। ये सिर्फ जोड़ने वाली जगह नहीं हैं; ये पूरे Coal Handling Plant में सबसे critical और सबसे hazardous locations हैं। CHP जाने से पहले यह समझना ज़रूरी है कि transfer point पर क्या होता है। BC-1 (Upper Conveyor) Coal on BC-1 Head Pulley TRANSFER CHUTE (coal को guide करती है) Coal गिरती है BC-2 (Lower Conveyor) Impact Zone Coal on BC-2 DUST Spillage Spillage BLOCKAGE RISK Wet/sticky coal chute block कर सकती है Coal को BC-2 belt के centre पर land होना चाहिए। कोई भी deviation — spillage या belt drift।

content: Skirt Boards और Dust Suppression Skirt boards feed/transfer zone पर belt के दोनों तरफ की side plates हैं जो coal को belt पर रोकती हैं। Rubber sealing strips belt surface के साथ contact में रहती हैं। अगर skirt gap 6 mm से ज़्यादा हो जाए — coal फिसलकर structure पर गिरती है। Skirt gap को हर shift में check करें। Dust suppression के तरीके: water mist sprays, foam suppression, dry fog systems। Enclosed areas में dust extraction (DE) system भी होता है जो dusty air को bag filters की तरफ खींचता है। Transfer point पर हमेशा N95 या बेहतर respirator पहनें।

content: Coal Dust और CWP Coal dust के लंबे समय तक exposure से Coal Workers' Pneumoconiosis (CWP) होता है — 'black lung disease' — एक irreversible और potentially fatal lung disease। इसका कोई इलाज नहीं है; सिर्फ prevention काम करती है। Respirator: N95 minimum; P100 preferred। Coal dust — air में 35–2,000 g/m³ concentration पर — ignite होने पर explode भी कर सकती है।

content: Fire का खतरा Fire sources: seized idler bearing friction, drive pulley पर belt slip, accumulated spill coal, electrical fault। Belt material (rubber) combustible होती है। Enclosed galleries में toxic smoke तेज़ी से भर जाती है। Prevention: हर shift में spill coal साफ करें, idlers की free rotation check करें, scrapers maintain करें। Gallery में fire हो तो: तुरंत evacuate करें, CO₂/DCP use करें।

content: Wagon Tippler के प्रकार Wagon Tippler coal का front door है — raw material पहली बार यहीं system में enter करती है। Tippler की capacity और availability directly determine करती है कि plant को कितनी coal supply होगी। Coal power plants में coal रेलवे wagons में आती है। हर wagon में लगभग 65–90 tonnes coal होती है। इन wagons को Wagon Tipplers के ज़रिए खाली किया जाता है, जो coal को hoppers में dump करती हैं, और वहाँ से Belt Conveyor No. 1 पर load होती है। Rotary Tippler Wagon (65-90 t) ~160° rotation Hopper (नीचे) Side Discharge Tippler Wagon tilts ~50° to one side Coal Side Hopper Simpler mechanism Lower capacity plants Track Hopper System BOXN-HL Wagon (bottom doors खुली) Track Hopper Pit (100–200 m लंबी) Gravity discharge No tipping mechanism Feeder → Belt No. 1

content: Rotary Tippler काम कैसे करता है: Coal wagon (65–90 t) को एक rotating cradle में clamp करके लगभग 160° घुमाया जाता है। Coal नीचे के hopper में dump होती है। Wagon rail से connected रहती है (knuckle couplers के ज़रिए)। Cycle time: 3–4 minutes/wagon Capacity: Single: ~1,000–1,200 TPH; Tandem (2 wagons एकसाथ): ~2,000 TPH कहाँ use होता है: Large thermal power plants (500 MW और ऊपर)
title: Rotary Tippler

breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training (Hindi)

content: Side Discharge Tippler काम कैसे करता है: Wagon को sideways (~50°) tilt किया जाता है — पूरा नहीं घुमाया। Coal एक तरफ के hopper में discharge होती है। Simpler mechanism — construction और maintenance easier। Capacity: ~500–800 TPH (rotary से कम) Limitation: सिर्फ side-discharge capable wagons के लिए। Large TPPs में इसे rotary से replace किया जा रहा है।
title: Side Discharge Tippler

breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training (Hindi)

content: Track Hopper System काम कैसे करता है: Rail tracks के नीचे concrete pit (hopper) बनी होती है। BOXN-HL type के bottom-discharge wagons के bottom doors खुलते हैं — coal gravity से नीचे गिरती है। Length: 100–200 m — एकसाथ 10–20 wagons handle करती है। Feed Control: Apron Feeder या Vibratory Feeder coal को regulate करके Belt No. 1 पर डालता है। Advantage: Low maintenance — कोई tipping mechanism नहीं। आपको Tippler को operate नहीं करना है — यह specialized work है। लेकिन आपको यह जानना है कि Wagon Tippler rate directly Belt Conveyor No. 1 की load को determine करती है । अगर tippler बहुत तेज़ unload कर रहा है, Belt 1 overloaded हो जाएगी। अगर tippler रुक जाए, पूरी coal supply chain रुक जाती है। इसीलिए यह पूरे system का starting point है।
title: Track Hopper System

content: Coal Loading onto Belt (Feed Point) कहाँ है: Tail pulley के ठीक बाद — जहाँ hopper/feeder से coal चलती हुई belt पर गिर रही है। यहाँ क्या critical है: Coal को belt के exactly centre में गिरना चाहिए — एक controlled rate पर (rated TPH से ज़्यादा नहीं), और free-fall height minimum होनी चाहिए ताकि impact और dust दोनों कम हों। Skirt boards को edges पर tight seal बनाना चाहिए coal को रोकने के लिए। अगर skirt board में कोई भी gap हो — तो सीधा spillage होगा। CP-1 पर overloading से belt sag होगी, edges से spillage होगी, और motor overload हो सकता है। Blocked skirt boards से belt edge damage होती है। Feed point पर बड़े coal lumps का impact belt cover को damage करता है।
title: Coal Loading onto Belt (Feed Point)

content: Transfer Between Conveyors (Transfer Point) कहाँ है: Transfer tower — जहाँ BC-1 से coal discharge होती है और chute के through BC-2 पर load होती है। यहाँ क्या critical है: Chute से गुज़रने वाली coal का trajectory receiving belt की speed और direction के साथ match होना चाहिए। Coal को BC-2 पर centrally land करना चाहिए। Chute blockage-free होनी चाहिए। Chute liners (wear-resistant steel plates) intact होने चाहिए। Deflector plates coal को accurately direct करें। यह पूरे CHP में सबसे high-risk location है। यहाँ blockages chute को back-fill कर सकती हैं, जिससे BC-1 overload होती है। यहाँ से spillage height से गिरती है। Dust maximum होती है। यहाँ confined space entry के लिए formal permit ज़रूरी है।
title: Transfer Between Conveyors (Transfer Point)

content: Belt Movement at Drive Pulley कहाँ है: Conveyor का head end — drive pulley, motor, और gearbox assembly। यहाँ क्या critical है: Drive pulley को belt के साथ sufficient friction maintain करनी चाहिए ताकि slipping के बिना motor torque transmit हो सके। Belt को pulley पर correct arc (wrap angle) पर wrap होना चाहिए। Head scraper को discharge होते वक्त belt surface से coal effectively remove करना चाहिए। Belt coal को cleanly नीचे की chute में discharge करे। Drive pulley पर belt slip = ZSS trip + heat generation → fire। Drive end पर carryback coal का accumulation idler damage और fire risk दोनों पैदा करता है। Worn scraper blades = excessive carryback।
title: Belt Movement at Drive Pulley

content: Belt Tracking Along the Full Length कहाँ है: Conveyor की पूरी length — हर idler frame पर belt की centreline position। यहाँ क्या critical है: Belt को सभी idlers पर centrally run करना चाहिए — दोनों तरफ equal clearance के साथ। Belt drift — एक तरफ को run करना — structure के against belt edge rubbing, edge fraying, और अंत में belt failure की तरफ ले जाती है। Self-aligning idlers छोटे drift को correct करते हैं। Belt drift → BSW alarm (stage 1) → conveyor trip (stage 2) अगर uncorrected रहे। ±50 mm drift पर alarm, ±75 mm पर trip। Running belt को manually push करके कभी correct नहीं करें।
title: Belt Tracking Along the Full Length

content: Bunker Discharge Point कहाँ है: Belt conveyor का tail end — जहाँ conveyor coal को bunker में discharge करती है (tripper car या fixed chute के through)। यहाँ क्या critical है: Bunker levels सभी bunkers में balanced रहनी चाहिए। Tripper car को sequentially move करना चाहिए coal को evenly distribute करने के लिए। Belt weigher data control room को confirm करे कि coal transfer हो रही है। Over-filling से coal belt पर back up होती है। Full bunker में coal discharge करने की कोशिश → coal belt पर backup → overloading → belt trip। Low bunker level के लिए level sensors coal supply को automatically trigger करते हैं। Tail Drive CP1 CP2 CP3 CP4 CP5 Feed Point Loading Transfer Point Chute junction Belt Alignment Full length Bunker Discharge Tripper car Drive Pulley Motor/Gearbox end CP1 से CP5 तक — हर shift में operator का inspection round इन्हीं points पर focus करता है। इन पाँच control points को याद कर लें — CP1 (Feed), CP2 (Transfer), CP3 (Drive), CP4 (Alignment), CP5 (Discharge)। Site visit पर supervisor आपसे पूछेंगे: "यहाँ क्या देखते हो?" अगर आप इन points को identify कर सकते हैं और यह बता सकते हैं कि वहाँ क्या check करना है — तो आप किसी भी दूसरे intern से आगे होंगे।

content: Belt Drift (Belt Misalignment) Root Cause: Off-centre loading (feeder से coal belt के center में नहीं गिर रही), worn idlers, wet/sticky coal जो एक तरफ build-up कर रही हो, misaligned pulleys, या incorrect take-up tension। Effect: Belt एक तरफ रगड़ती है conveyor structure से → belt edge fraying → material spillage → structure damage → fire risk (friction से)। Detection: BSW (Belt Sway Switch) alarm; visual patrol में belt edge की position देखें। Immediate Action: Feed rate कम करें → self-aligning idlers adjust करें → loading pattern investigate करें। BSW trip के बाद investigation के बिना restart नहीं।
title: Belt Drift (Belt Misalignment)

breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training (Hindi)

content: Belt Overloading Root Cause: Feeder gate ज़रूरत से ज़्यादा खुली, wet/dense coal (higher bulk density), multiple feeders simultaneously over-feeding, या belt speed design से कम। Effect: Coal belt के sides से spill होती है → idler frames overloaded → bearing failure → motor overload trip → conveyor stop। Detection: Belt Weigher पर high TPH reading; visual spillage; motor current high alarm। Immediate Action: Feeder gate कम करें → Belt Weigher reading monitor करें → spilled coal साफ करें → idlers inspect करें।
title: Belt Overloading

breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training (Hindi)

content: Chute Blockage (Choking) Root Cause: Wet/sticky coal जो chute opening में bridge बनाती है, oversized lumps (crusher bypass), worn liners जो flow area reduce कर देती हैं, या low belt speed। Effect: Coal chute में backup होती है → upstream belt पर load बढ़ता है → ZSS trip downstream belt पर → production stoppage। Detection: Chute Blocked Detector alarm; coal backup देखना upstream belt पर; downstream belt पर ZSS trip। Immediate Action: Upstream belt/feeder stop करें FIRST (coal supply cut करें) → chute के बाहर से vibrator या rod use करें → कभी भी हाथ अंदर मत डालें → LOTO mandatory किसी भी manual entry से पहले।
title: Chute Blockage (Choking)

breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training (Hindi)

content: Belt Slip Root Cause: Low belt tension (worn/slack take-up), glazed या oily drive pulley surface, wet belt surface, severe overloading। Effect: Drive pulley rotate करता है लेकिन belt full speed से move नहीं करती → ZSS trip होता है → extreme heat drive pulley contact point पर → belt cover melt होती है → fire ignites spill coal। Detection: ZSS trip (speed drop); drive end पर rubber burning smell; drive pulley पर rubber streak marks। Immediate Action: EPC या ZSS trip के बाद तुरंत stop → drive area inspect करें for heat/fire → tension check करें, pulley surface inspect करें, load check करें → fire हो तो evacuate, FAS activate करें।
title: Belt Slip

breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training (Hindi)

content: Dust Accumulation Fire Root Cause: Spill coal का belt structure के नीचे accumulation, seized idler bearing जो enough heat generate करती है ignition के लिए, poor housekeeping, absent या non-functional thermal detector। Effect: Gallery fire → belt total destruction → structural damage → toxic smoke → production loss कई दिनों का। Detection: Thermal detector alarm; burning smell; smoke; seized idler की squealing sound। Immediate Action: EPC pull → Fire Alarm System activate → gallery तुरंत evacuate → CO₂ या DCP extinguisher use करें — live electrical equipment पर कभी water नहीं। Emergency response team को call करें।
title: Dust Accumulation Fire

breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training (Hindi)

content: Entanglement Injury Root Cause: Running conveyor पर LOTO के बिना काम करना, nip point के पास loose clothing/hair, bypassed या removed guards। Effect: Crush injury, amputation, या fatal outcome। Nip points पर यह 1 second से कम में होता है। EPC pull करने की speed भी insufficient होती है एक बार contact हो जाए। Detection: यह preventable है — detect करके नहीं, prevent करके। EPC pull होगा लेकिन तब तक बहुत देर हो सकती है। Prevention (Prevention = Action): LOTO हर बार, हर काम से पहले — कोई exception नहीं। Close-fitting workwear हमेशा। Guards कभी remove नहीं करें — अगर missing हो तो report करें और belt तब तक run मत करें। Notice करें: हर failure case एक pattern follow करता है — एक condition (जो कुछ समय से build हो रही थी) + एक trigger (जो उसे failure में convert करती है) । इसीलिए preventive inspection rounds — जहाँ आप conditions को deteriorate होते देखते हैं — उतने ही important हैं जितने emergency responses। एक अच्छा operator failure को होने से पहले identify करता है।
title: Entanglement Injury

Drive Pulley | Powered pulley जो motor से belt को friction के through move करती है — conveyor का head end ; Tail Pulley | Unpowered pulley जो opposite end पर है — belt यहाँ से return side में जाती है ; Idler | Freely rotating roller जो belt को support करता है — carry side पर troughed set में, return side पर flat ; Take-up System | Mechanism (gravity weight या screw) जो belt tension को maintain करता है — slip और sag दोनों prevent करता है ; Belt Scraper | Primary और secondary blades जो drive pulley पर belt की outer face से carryback coal remove करती हैं ; Skirt Board | Feed/transfer zone पर belt के sides पर side plates जो coal को belt पर contain करती हैं ; Transfer Chute | Steel duct जो coal को एक belt से दूसरी belt पर guide करती है ; EPC (Emergency Pull Cord) | Rope switch जो full conveyor length में होती है — कहीं से भी pull करने पर instant stop और self-latch ; BSW (Belt Sway Switch) | Belt drift detect करता है — stage 1 alarm, stage 2 trip ; ZSS (Zero Speed Switch) | Belt speed monitor करता है — speed drop → auto trip (belt slip detect करने के लिए) ; Belt Weigher | Gravimetric instrument जो real-time TPH measure करता है — load cell + speed sensor ; Tight Side | Drive pulley से exit होने वाली belt side — high tension (T1) ; Slack Side | Drive pulley में enter होने वाली belt side — low tension (T2) ; Trough Angle | Carry idlers का angle जो belt को V-shape में form करता है — 35° standard, 45° high-capacity ; TPH (Tonnes Per Hour) | Coal conveying rate की unit — plant की demand के हिसाब से control किया जाता है ; LOTO (Lockout-Tagout) | Safety procedure: personal padlock + tag से equipment को isolate करना maintenance से पहले ; Nip Point | Belt और rotating pulley के बीच converging gap — extremely dangerous — entanglement का point ; CWP (Coal Workers' Pneumoconiosis) | Coal dust से होने वाली chronic lung disease — Black Lung — irreversible ; Carryback | Coal जो belt के outer face से discharge होने के बाद भी चिपकी रहती है — structure पर गिरती है ; Impact Idler | Rubber-cushioned idler जो feed/transfer point पर coal के impact को absorb करती है ; Rotary Tippler | Wagon को cradle में clamp करके ~160° rotate करने वाला machine — coal hopper में dump करता है ; Track Hopper | Rail tracks के नीचे का concrete pit — BOXN-HL wagons के bottom doors से gravity discharge होता है ; Crusher House | Building जहाँ coal को ≤50 mm तक crush किया जाता है — mill feed requirement के लिए ; Bunker | Coal mills के ऊपर का large storage vessel — 8–12 hours mill feed hold करता है ; Thermal Detector | Rate-of-rise या fixed-point temperature sensor — fire detection के लिए; FAS से connected ; Chute Blocked Detector | Rotary paddle या RF type sensor जो chute fill-up detect करता है — upstream belt trip करता है ; Belt Drift | Belt का centreline से lateral wander — BSW alarm/trip को trigger करता है ; Wear Liner | Chute के अंदर WR steel या UHMWPE के replaceable panels — abrasion से protect करते हैं ; PLF (Plant Load Factor) | Actual generation / Rated capacity — conveyor availability directly PLF को affect करती है ; Fluid Coupling | Motor और gearbox के बीच hydraulic coupling — start-up shock absorb करती है, smooth start देती है ; Confined Space | Enclosed या restricted space जैसे chute, hopper, bunker — entry के लिए formal permit mandatory है

content: Control Point 1 — Pre-Start System Readiness Check The downstream belt conveyor must be confirmed running and at the correct speed before feeder start is commanded. This confirmation comes from the control room or from the supervisor who has checked belt status on the SCADA/PLC system. As a trainee, you do not have the authority or system access to confirm belt status — this is a supervisor action. Your role: Stand at the feeder local panel area, observe the feeder visually, and listen for the supervisor's instruction to proceed. Do not touch the start pushbutton unless specifically directed. Before start, the hopper should have sufficient coal to sustain initial flow. You can assist by checking the hopper level indicator (if visible locally) or reading the level gauge and reporting the reading to your supervisor. Low hopper level may cause intermittent feeding — important to note before starting. What to report: Hopper level reading. Presence of any blockage at the hopper throat. Any unusual odours or visible smoke from the hopper area (can indicate spontaneous combustion). Confirm that no personnel are in the feeder zone — under the feeder trough, near the discharge end, or inside the underground hopper area. Both you and your supervisor walk the immediate zone before any start command is issued. This is a procedural safety step and is never skipped regardless of time pressure.
title: Control Point 1 — Pre-Start System Readiness Check

content: Common Mistakes in Assisted Execution These are the execution errors that occur most often among trainees during their first supervised interactions with feeder systems. They are not listed to make you nervous — they are listed so you recognise the pattern if you start heading toward it. Mistake | Why It Happens | Consequence | Severity ; Touching the start button before supervisor confirms system readiness | Eagerness to help; mistaking presence of button for permission to use it | Feeder starts before downstream belt is ready; spillage or belt trip | HIGH ; Standing in the coal discharge fall zone during observation | Wanting a better viewing angle; not knowing the designated safe observation point | Coal impact injury; coal dust inhalation; being caught in moving material | HIGH ; Treating inspection as a quick visual pass — not pausing to observe carefully | Time pressure; assumption that nothing will be wrong | Hazardous material (tramp iron, oversized coal) enters the system undetected | HIGH ; Not reporting an early warning condition because "it seems minor" | Self-doubt; not wanting to raise a false alarm; not knowing what normal is | Small issues become failures; early warning missed means later incident | HIGH ; Walking away from the feeder during the post-start observation window | Feeling that once it starts, the job is done | Abnormal behaviour in the first 60 seconds goes undetected | MEDIUM ; Not accounting for inertia during a stop — assuming coal stops when the motor stops | Intuition from everyday experience (switches turn things off instantly) | Misreads the discharge end as clear when coal is still flowing; wrong report | MEDIUM ; Attempting to remove obstruction from the feeder trough | Wanting to solve the problem; not wanting to slow things down | Entanglement injury; crush injury; falls into trough | CRITICAL / FATAL

content: Why a feeder is needed Without a feeder, coal in the hopper would rush out uncontrollably — sometimes flooding the conveyor, sometimes blocking and stopping entirely. ℹ Mental Model Two main types of feeders are used in track hopper systems — Belt Feeders and Apron Feeders . content: Apron Feeder HOPPER → Overlapping steel pan chain Heavy-duty · handles large lumps Apron Feeder — chain of overlapping steel pans for heavy-duty, coarse-coal applications

content: ✅ Strengths Handles very large lumps and heavy loads. No belt to cut. Robust construction.

content: Coal is NOT a liquid Most people assume coal flows like water. It doesn't. Coal is a bulk solid — it flows, yes, but it also stops, bridges, jams, and collapses suddenly . ℹ Key Behaviour Patterns Both arch formation and surge flow are dangerous — for equipment and for people nearby. Swipe to understand each one.
title: Coal is NOT a liquid

content: Arch Formation — The Silent Stop Coal above arch ARCH (bridge) ⛔ Flow STOPS Coal above builds up · pressure increases Arch formation — coal bridges the outlet, all flow stops. Pressure above increases silently. 💧 More likely with wet, fine, or clay-rich coal ❄️ Increases in winter — moisture freezes, coal compacts ⏰ Static storage — coal that sits too long settles and bridges
title: Arch Formation — The Silent Stop

content: Surge Flow — The Sudden Collapse ⬇⬇⬇ SUDDEN SURGE — massive coal rush Arch collapses → ALL backed-up coal rushes out at once, flooding feeder and conveyor 🚨 The Deadly Risk

content: Wagon Unloading Over Hopper Coal is officially entering the plant here. Wagon bottom doors open over the grizzly. The interaction between heavy rail movement and an open pit is the defining hazard at this control point. ⚠ Risks at CP1 🚨 Zone Rule

content: Grizzly & Accumulation Every piece of coal gets size-classified here. Broken bars = unprotected feeder. Inspect after every unloading, never during. Tramp material on bars must be removed safely. The hopper buffers between variable wagon discharge rate and steady feeder rate. Overfill → coal at grizzly level (fall hazard). Underfill with arch → surge when it fails. Both extremes are dangerous.
title: Grizzly & Accumulation
parent_title: 5 Critical Points in the Coal Chain

content: Feeder & To Conveyor The feeder operates under the full weight of coal above pressing down. Restarting under a full hopper needs significantly more torque than normal — this is why feeder motors are oversized. Feeder zone is underground and inaccessible during operation. This is where the Track Hopper system meets the rest of the CHP. Feeder rate must match conveyor capacity. Overloading trips the conveyor — instantly halting all downstream coal flow to boiler bunkers.
